transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Hi, yeah, thanks for having me. Well, I guess... it’s a bit of a long story, but the main thing that brings me in is that I just feel like I’m always, always moving from one thing to the next. Like I really can’t just sit and idle, you know? 

I’ve been a customer service rep for a long time, and I used to be able to kind of manage it on my own. I'd be on the headset and I could pace around a bit, or I'd be shifting around at my desk, just keeping myself in motion while I talked to people on the phone. But recently, the company changed our whole work setup. They moved us to this open-plan office thing—no more high cubicle walls, everyone can see everyone else, and the supervisors are right there just looking across the floor. 

And with this new setup, it’s made it a lot harder to hide. I can't just get up and pace anymore without people staring, but I still have that feeling where I just can't sit still, and I'm constantly shifting or trying to bounce to the next thing. It’s just... it’s becoming a real problem at work now because I can't fly under the radar with it like I used to, and it's exhausting trying to force myself to just sit quietly like everyone else does.

Can you tell me how far back this restlessness and difficulty sitting still goes—did you notice it as far back as childhood, or is this something that started more recently, say within the last few years?

Well, you know, it’s funny you ask that, because when this whole office change happened and I started really struggling with having to just sit there in my chair, I started thinking back on it. And, well, no, it's definitely not just the last few years. Not at all. I mean, looking back, this has been around long before this job change, long before I even started working in customer service, honestly. 

I remember way back in grade school—and this is going back a long time, obviously, I'm 57 now—but I remember my parents used to get these report cards, and the teachers would always write these little notes on them. They were always the same, year after year. They'd say I was bright, which, you know, was nice to hear, but then they'd always follow it up with how I was careless with my assignments. And the talking—oh boy, they always mentioned the talking. I talked out of turn constantly. I just couldn't seem to hold onto a thought without blurting it out right then and there. 

And they always had to remind me to stay with my work. I'd be doing a worksheet or whatever, and then something else would catch my eye, or I'd just get this urge to get up, and the teacher would have to come over and tap my desk and tell me to focus. It was just a constant thing. So, yeah, it’s not new. It’s just that, for a long time, I found ways to work around it, you know? Like with the headset and pacing. But now that I can't do that, it feels exactly like being back in that grade school classroom, having to just sit there when every part of me wants to be moving or doing something else. It's incredibly frustrating, to be honest.
Are you currently taking any medications, such as antipsychotics, anti-nausea drugs, or other prescriptions, that you started around the time this restlessness became more noticeable?

No, no, I'm not taking anything like that. I mean, I take a multivitamin sometimes, when I remember to buy them at the grocery store, but no real prescription medications. Definitely no antipsychotics or anti-nausea things. It's funny you mention medications, though, because when this whole open-office thing started and I was feeling so antsy, I actually wondered if maybe I was drinking too much coffee. Because, you know, they have that big industrial coffee maker in the break room now, and it's free, so I'd find myself going over there just to have an excuse to walk away from my desk. I thought, well, maybe it's the caffeine making me jittery. So I switched to decaf for a whole month—which, let me tell you, decaf from those machines tastes like hot dirt—but it didn't make a lick of difference. I was still just as squirmy in my chair, still feeling that motor running inside me. So, yeah, it's definitely not a medication thing, and not a caffeine thing either, as far as I can tell. It's just... me, I guess. It's always just been me.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a lifelong (since childhood) pattern of both hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (motor restlessness, inability to sit still, need to be in constant motion, blurting out answers/talking out of turn) and inattentive symptoms (carelessness with assignments, distractibility, difficulty sustaining attention), documented as early as grade school via teacher reports. Symptoms have persisted into adulthood (age 57) and are currently causing functional impairment at work due to environmental changes (open-plan office removing prior compensatory strategies like pacing). Medication use and caffeine were ruled out as causes (trialed decaf, no antipsychotic/stimulant use), excluding substance-induced restlessness or akathisia. The combined presence of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptom clusters across the lifespan with cross-situational impairment supports ADHD, Combined Type (F90.2) over predominantly inattentive (F90.0) or predominantly hyperactive-impulsive (F90.1) subtypes.
